Asymptotic Variance of the Coefficient of Variation

Source: R/var_cv.R
var_cv.Rd

Computes the large-sample variance of the sample coefficient of variation \(k = s / M\), the sample standard deviation divided by the sample mean, for a random sample from a normal population: \(\kappa^2 (1/2 + \kappa^2) / (N - 1)\). It takes the population coefficient of variation and the sample size and returns the variance. Companion to ci_cv and ss_aipe_cv.

Usage

var_cv(true_cv, N)

Arguments

true_cv

Population coefficient of variation \(\kappa = \sigma / \mu\). A single finite number greater than 0. For \(\kappa\) above about 0.4 the value returned is too small, and more so the larger \(\kappa\) is (see Details); for an interval use ci_cv, which does not use this variance.

N

Total sample size. A single finite number of at least 3.

Value

A data.frame with the columns term and value and one row, var_cv_normal: the first-order variance of the sample coefficient of variation under normality (see Details).

Details

Estimand. The variance, over repeated samples of \(N\) independent observations from a normal population with mean \(\mu > 0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), of the sample coefficient of variation \(k = s / M\), evaluated at the population value \(\kappa = \sigma / \mu\) given as true_cv. Strictly, the sample coefficient has no finite variance, because the sample mean can be arbitrarily close to zero; the expression below describes its spread when that event has negligible probability, that is, when \(\sqrt{N} / \kappa\) is large. Substituting a sample coefficient for true_cv gives a plug-in estimate of the variance, which carries the sampling error of the coefficient it was computed from.

The variance. The first-order (delta method) variance is $$\mathrm{Var}(k) \;\approx\; \frac{\kappa^2}{N - 1} \left(\frac{1}{2} + \kappa^2\right).$$ It follows from \(\mathrm{Var}(s) \approx \sigma^2 / \{2 (N - 1)\}\), \(\mathrm{Var}(M) = \sigma^2 / N\), and the independence of \(s\) and \(M\) under normality, which give \(\mathrm{Var}(k) \approx \kappa^2 / \{2 (N - 1)\} + \kappa^4 / N\). That expression is Expression 5 of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 52) without its third-order term. The function uses \(N - 1\) under both terms, which agrees with it to first order in \(1/N\) and is larger by \(\kappa^4 / \{N (N - 1)\}\). The form usually given, their Expression 7, has \(N\) under both terms: \(\kappa^2 (1/2 + \kappa^2) / N\).

Accuracy under normality. The comparisons in this paragraph are with the variance of \(k\) when the sample mean is restricted to lie within 8 standard errors of \(\mu\) and to be at least \(\mu / 50\). The restriction excludes a probability below \(10^{-9}\) in every case reported, and the figures given are the same for any lower bound from \(\mu / 1000\) to \(\mu / 5\). For \(\kappa \le 0.3\) and \(N \ge 10\) the value is too large. The excess is largest for a small \(\kappa\), where it is that of \(\sigma^2 / \{2 (N - 1)\}\) over the exact variance of \(s\): to one decimal place, 3.0 percent at \(N = 10\), 1.4 percent at \(N = 20\), 0.9 percent at \(N = 30\), and 0.5 percent at \(N = 50\). For \(\kappa\) above about 0.4 the value is too small, because of the terms of higher order that a first-order variance omits: by 5.7 percent at \(\kappa = 0.5\) and \(N = 10\), and by 1.7 percent at \(\kappa = 0.5\) and \(N = 30\).

Normality. The value is for a normal population. For any population with a finite fourth moment, the large-sample variance of \(k\) is \(\xi^2 / N\), with $$\xi^2 \;=\; \frac{\kappa^2}{2} + \kappa^4 - \kappa^3 \gamma_1 + \frac{\kappa^2 \gamma_2}{4},$$ where \(\gamma_1\) is the skewness and \(\gamma_2\) the excess kurtosis of the population (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018, Equation 30, which is written in central moments). Under normality both are 0 and \(\xi^2 = \kappa^2 (1/2 + \kappa^2)\). For other populations the normal-theory value can be far off in either direction: \(\kappa^2 (1/2 + \kappa^2)\) is 39 percent larger than \(\xi^2\) for a gamma population with \(\kappa = 0.8\), and 56 percent smaller for a Laplace (double exponential) population with \(\kappa = 0.3\). These compare the limiting values, so a larger sample does not remove the difference. mr_cv estimates \(\xi^2\) from the scores, without assuming a normal population.

Use. Neither ci_cv nor ss_aipe_cv uses this variance: the interval inverts the noncentral t distribution of \(\sqrt{N} / k\), and the planner (Kelley, 2007) chooses the sample size for that interval. The value serves as a quick description of the sampling variability of \(k\) and for comparison with a simulated variance. McKay (1932) and Vangel (1996) approximate the distribution of a function of \(k\) by a chi square distribution, from which confidence limits follow; the variance here is not taken from those approximations.

References

Kelley, K. (2007). Sample size planning for the coefficient of variation from the accuracy in parameter estimation approach. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 755–766. doi:10.3758/BF03192966

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

McKay, A. T. (1932). Distribution of the coefficient of variation and the extended t distribution. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 95(4), 695–698.

Sokal, R. R., & Braumann, C. A. (1980). Significance tests for coefficients of variation and variability profiles. Systematic Zoology, 29(1), 50–66. doi:10.1093/sysbio/29.1.50

Vangel, M. G. (1996). Confidence intervals for a normal coefficient of variation. The American Statistician, 50(1), 21–26. doi:10.1080/00031305.1996.10473537

Examples

# The variance of the sample coefficient of variation in samples of 30
# from a normal population whose coefficient is .20. The variance is
# small, so it is printed to six decimal places.
v <- var_cv(true_cv = 0.20, N = 30)
print(v, digits = 6)
#>  term          value   
#>  var_cv_normal 0.000745

# Its square root is the standard error of the sample coefficient, shown
# here beside the standard deviation of 2000 simulated coefficients.
set.seed(113)
k <- replicate(2000, {
  y <- rnorm(30, mean = 10, sd = 2)
  sd(y) / mean(y)
})
c(normal_theory = sqrt(v$value), simulated = sd(k))
#> normal_theory     simulated 
#>    0.02729153    0.02689039 

# The same comparison for a skewed population, a gamma distribution
# with a coefficient of .80 and samples of 200: the normal-theory
# standard error is too large.
k_gamma <- replicate(2000, {
  y <- rgamma(200, shape = 1 / 0.80^2)
  sd(y) / mean(y)
})
c(normal_theory = sqrt(var_cv(true_cv = 0.80, N = 200)$value),
  simulated = sd(k_gamma))
#> normal_theory     simulated 
#>    0.06055024    0.05082959
